entities.name: Central African Federation
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Central African Federation (CAF), also known as the Federation of Rhodesia and Nyasaland (1953-1963), was the political union imposed by the British Colonial Office on Northern Rhodesia (Zambia), Southern Rhodesia (Zimbabwe), and Nyasaland (Malawi) — a federation that African populations in all three territories overwhelmingly opposed from its inception as representing white settler political domination under British colonial architecture, and whose dissolution after a decade proved that African majority opposition to colonial political structures could succeed.

The Federation was imposed despite almost universal African opposition, particularly from Nyasaland's Congress movement led by Dr. Hastings Banda (who returned from exile to lead the Nyasaland African Congress in 1958). Britain's Devlin Report (1959) — commissioned after the 1959 State of Emergency crackdown on African nationalist protests — memorably described Nyasaland as 'a police state.' The Monckton Commission (1960) recommended that territories should have the right to secede.

Nyasaland under Banda was the first to negotiate independence, with Malawi gaining independence on July 6, 1964. Northern Rhodesia followed as Zambia in October 1964. Southern Rhodesia's white minority government declared Unilateral Declaration of Independence (UDI) in 1965 — the crisis that would take another 15 years to resolve through guerrilla war and Lancaster House Agreement (1979). The CAF's failure and dissolution demonstrated that British colonial administrators could not impose multiracial but white-dominated federal structures against African nationalist will — a crucial precedent for subsequent decolonization.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Central African Federation — the British colonial-imposed white-dominated union that three African nationalist movements dismantled, whose dissolution led to Malawi, Zambia independence, and the Southern Rhodesia UDI crisis that took 15 more years to resolve — is one of the most significant colonial political structures in African decolonization history.
